extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientists interested in foundations of induction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and forming inductive inferences and scientific laws: what counts as sufficient evidence, how to treat generalization, how to relate particular inductions to broader laws, and what methodological safeguards (experiments, surveys, consistency checks) are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of the course of nature (axiom of induction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposition that the course of nature is uniform is the fundamental principle, or general axiom of Induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this as the ultimate major premise one supplies in inductive syllogisms: it is a necessary condition for inductive proof (not itself an explanation). Note the author regards this principle as itself an instance of induction rather than an a priori certainty; it should be justified by prior generalizations rather than invoked as an independent ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference from known to unknown (not merely past→future)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction proceeds from facts observed to facts unobserved — from the known to the unknown — and not simply from the past to the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating inductive claims, check whether the inference is really from directly observed kinds of facts to unobserved ones (including unobserved pasts and remote places) and whether the categories being transferred are genuinely comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductio per enumerationem simplicem is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The crude ancient form of induction — ascribing general truth to a proposition that is true in every known instance (simple enumeration) — is usually insufficient for scientific purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid concluding universality merely because all known instances agree. Seek contradictory instances actively and do not rely on passive acceptance of presented facts; experiment and targeted observation are required to strengthen such generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major premise suppression and syllogistic formulation of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Every induction may be thrown into the form of a syllogism by supplying a major premise (often suppressed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit the general premise that links observed cases to the general conclusion (e.g., 'what is true of these observed cases is true of all cases of that kind') and scrutinize the grounds for that major premise rather than accepting it implicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: The axiom of uniformity must itself be supported by prior generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of the uniformity of nature is itself founded on prior generalizations — it is not our earliest induction but one of the later, more general inductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using uniformity as a justification, demand account of the prior inductions that make it credible. Do not treat uniformity as an unexplained a priori necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class-specific reliability of uniformities
rubrics_metrics.description: Some classes of phenomena exhibit more dependable uniformity than others (e.g., anatomical structure vs. animal coloration); induction’s force depends on the kind of case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess inductive strength by reference to the type/class of phenomenon: ask whether that class has historically shown stable uniformities, and weigh generalizations accordingly (swans vs. human anatomy example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-instance sufficiency depends on context and prior knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases (e.g., a chemist’s properly conducted experiment) a single instance may suffice for a universal conclusion; in other cases even many instances may be weak evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether a single observation is probative by considering plausibility given background theory, method quality, and whether the phenomenon typically varies; distinguish between doubts about experiment execution and doubts about the idea that one instance could be conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompose complex regularities into simpler uniformities (laws vs. cases of laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: What vulgar speech calls 'laws' often are complex uniformities that may in truth be results of a few simpler, independent laws of nature; true 'laws of nature' are the simplest uniformities from which others may be deduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explanations that reduce many regularities to a few simple, independent laws. Evaluate whether a purported law is fundamental or merely a corollary of simpler laws (Torricellian example with three simpler uniformities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification by specific experience remains desirable even when deductive from simpler laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a complex uniformity is deduced from simpler laws, verification by specific experiment may still be desirable and sometimes indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not abandon empirical verification merely because a result follows deductively from accepted laws; check important deductions by experiment when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey historical inductions to learn which uniformities are reliable
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific formula of induction requires a survey of the inductions to which mankind have been conducted in unscientific practice, to ascertain which kinds of uniformities are perfectly invariable and which vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying inductive rules, consult the empirical record: identify which types of uniformities have shown stability or variability across time/place. This historical/empirical survey is an indispensable foundation for judging inductive strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stronger inductions as touchstones for weaker ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Stronger inductions are the touchstone to which weaker ones should be brought; if a weaker induction can be deduced from stronger ones its certainty rises to that of the weakest premise supporting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a new or weak generalization by attempting to connect it to better-established generalizations via ratiocination; successful deduction increases confidence and binds evidence together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual testing by inconsistency (conflict resolves to revision)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an induction conflicts with stronger inductions, or with conclusions correctly deduced from them, then one or the other must be given up or more guardedly expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for deductive incompatibilities among inductions; use conflicts to identify which generalizations require revision; prioritize retention of the better-established inductions unless their scope has been overstated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity is plural and compositional — analyze into partial uniformities
rubrics_metrics.description: The general regularity of nature is a complex tissue composed of many separate uniformities (partial regularities) which co-exist and combine to produce more complex regularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining or testing a phenomenon, attempt to unravel it into component uniformities; experimental rules should be aimed at isolating these threads to understand the composite regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active interrogation/experimentation versus passive observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncultivated observation is passive and accepts presented facts; scientific inquiry requires seeking necessary facts, experimenting, and 'interrogating nature' (Bacon’s method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor designed experiments and the deliberate search for relevant instances (including negative and contradictory cases) over passive accumulation of coincidences; plan observation to test specific hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of number and space have special, rigorous universality but cannot yield laws of succession alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of number and laws of space (geometry) exhibit the rigorous universality we seek, but from them alone we cannot deduce laws of succession; laws of succession require additional premises about temporal relations and forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mathematical/geometrical certainty as foundational but insufficient for explanations about temporal sequences or causal succession; to infer succession, combine spatial/arithmetical premises with empirical premises about how phenomena succeed one another.
